pages.title: Conceptual foundations of data scaling laws.
claims: Q: Why do scaling laws show up?
We know error should be monotone
But why is it a power law / linear in log-log?
A (?): Estimation error naturally decays polynomially.
But this answer may take a moment to understand. Let’s work through an example.
Example: If our task is to estimate the mean of a dataset, what’s the scaling law?

claims: Input: 𝑥1 … 𝑥𝑛 ∼ 𝑁(𝜇, 𝜎 2 )
Task: estimate the average as 𝜇ො =
What’s the error? By standard arguments..

More generally, any polynomial rate 1/𝑛 𝛼 is a scaling law

pages.title: Detour: scaling laws for (nonparametric) learning
claims: Neural nets can approximate arbitrary functions. Lets turn that into an example.
Input: 𝑥1 … 𝑥𝑛 uniform in 2D unit box. 𝑦𝑖 = 𝑓 𝑥𝑖 + 𝑁(0,1)
Task: estimate f(x)
Approach: cut up the 2D space into boxes with length 𝑛 −4
What’s our estimation error?
Informally, we have 𝑛 boxes, each box gets 𝑛 samples.
In 𝑑-dimensions, this becomes 𝐸𝑟𝑟𝑜𝑟 = 𝑛 −1/𝑑 - This means scaling is 𝒚 = − 𝒙 + 𝑪
Takeaway: flexible ‘nonparametric’ learning has dimension dependent scaling laws.

pages.title: Intrinsic dimensionality theory of data scaling laws
claims: Some have made the following argument (Bahri 2021)
1. Scaling laws arise due to polynomial rates of learning
2. Some argue the slope 𝛼 is closely connected to the intrinsic dimensionality of the data.
But estimators of intrinsic dimension are sketchy, and this is not airtight..

pages.title: Some surprising takeaways
claims: The effect of hyperparameters on big LMs can be predicted before training!
Optimizer choice
Model depth
Architecture choice
The scaling law based design procedure.
1. Train a few smaller models
2. Establish a scaling law (e.g. ADAM vs SGD scaling law)
3. Select optimal hyperparam based on the scaling law prediction.

pages.title: One important use of scaling laws
claims: Q: Do we need more data or bigger models?
Clearly, lots of data is wasted on small models
Joint data-model scaling laws describe how the two relate
𝐸𝑟𝑟𝑜𝑟 = 𝑚−𝛼 + 𝑛−1 𝛽
Provides surprisingly good fits to model-data joint error.

pages.title: ‘Optimal’ compute and data tradeoffs as a case study.
claims: Rosenfeld, Kaplan both predict relationship of data, model and perf.
Kaplan claims: 𝑁𝑜𝑝𝑡 = 𝐶 0.73 , 𝐷𝑜𝑝𝑡 = 𝐶 0.27 (tokens per param decreases w/ C)
Hoffman+ 2022
cites: Chinchilla [Hoffman et al] argue these fits are quite off.

pages.title: Chinchilla in depth – 3 methods
claims: The chinchilla authors suggest 3 ways of fitting scaling laws – we’ll go over each.
They mostly (minus method 3) suggest similar constants. More on this later..

pages.title: Method 1 – minimum over runs.
claims: the minimum over the union of all training curves is a power law.
figures_mentioned: Similar to the FLOPS figure on Kaplan –

pages.title: Method 2 - IsoFLOPS
claims: Pick a range of FLOP budgets, vary the total parameter count, take the min over these
convex shapes. The minima form a power law.

pages.title: Method 3 – Joint fits
claims: Run a bunch of models on the size-data grid. Use least squares to fit a joint scaling law

pages.title: Why do we have this big difference?
claims: Kaplan claims: 𝑁𝑜𝑝𝑡 = 𝐶 0.73 , 𝐷𝑜𝑝𝑡 = 𝐶 0.27 (tokens per param decreases w/ C)
Why such a big difference (when both fit joint scaling laws?)

pages.title: Explanation 1
claims: Kaplan removed last layer param from the count
Warmup at very small compute budgets was too high
(Decay itself is maybe not critical if batch / LR is properly tuned)

pages.title: Explanation 2
claims: Non-embedding vs total param choice + small nonlinearities

pages.title: Fun addendum – errors in chinchilla method 3
claims: Note that this method three was likely flawed in the original paper. Some authors did
data forensics, recovered the raw data, and re-did the fit and got results more
consistent with methods 1 and 2

pages.title: Important note – train-optimal is likely not what you want
claims: Chinchilla aims to tell you what gives the best model for fixed training compute..
But most of the compute in a real deployment is inference.. So we should ‘over’ train
GPT3 – 2 tokens / param
Chinchilla – 20 tokens / param
LLaMA65B – 22 tokens / param
Llama 2 70B – 29 tokens / param
Mistral 7B – 110 tokens / param
Llama 3 70B – 215 tokens / param
… etc etc
The more usage we expect, the more it becomes worth it to pay the upfront cost
